fields.explanation: An AP system answers from whatever replica the client can reach, so reads may be stale and two sides can accept conflicting writes. The bill arrives after the partition heals: something has to merge those versions, and last-write-wins silently discards one of them while version vectors hand the conflict back to the application. Blocking until every replica agrees is the consistency guarantee AP trades away.

problems: explanation is wrong about CRDTs: it lumps them with rules that 'either drop writes or force the application to resolve them', but a CRDT's defining property is a deterministic automatic merge with no application resolution step

evidence: knowledge: a CRDT defines a commutative, associative, idempotent merge so replicas converge without application-level conflict resolution (Shapiro et al., 'Conflict-free Replicated Data Types')
knowledge: Dynamo-style stores use version vectors to expose siblings for application resolution, or last-write-wins, which discards a concurrent update
notes: Amended explanation keeps the two examples that do carry the stated cost and drops the false CRDT claim.

fields.explanation: Nothing downstream depends on the exact count at a given instant, so replicas can take increments locally and converge, which is what makes sharded counters and per-region aggregation possible on a very hot write path. Insisting on strong consistency here buys nothing a user can perceive and adds a coordination round trip to the most frequent write in the product. The trade is workload-specific: the same relaxation applied to an account balance would be a defect.

fields.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is the status for a client that has sent too many requests in a given time, defined in RFC 6585 section 4, and it may carry a Retry-After header. 403 refuses the request outright rather than inviting a later attempt, 503 says the server itself is unavailable, and 504 says an upstream did not answer in time. The distinction is operational: 429 and 503 tell a caller that backing off and retrying is the right move, while 403 tells it to stop.

problems: explanation overstated the spec: 'usually carries a Retry-After header' is a frequency claim I cannot verify, and both RFC 6585 and MDN say only that the header may be included

knowledge: RFC 6585 section 4 defines 429 Too Many Requests and makes the Retry-After header optional
notes: Key and options are sound; the hint narrows by restating the scenario, which is fair scaffolding for a code-recall item.

evidence: url: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Retry-After - the value is an <http-date> or a non-negative <delay-seconds>; used with 503, 429 and 301 responses

fields.explanation: Queuing smooths a short spike, and that is its entire value: it moves work in time rather than removing it. The cost is latency and a growing queue, so a sustained overload turns into client timeouts and retries against work the server is still holding, which is why queues need a bounded depth and a shed-on-full rule. Rejecting immediately with 429 is cheaper and lets the client back off with a Retry-After. Check what a product actually does: AWS API Gateway calls its limiter throttling but rejects with 429 rather than queuing.

problems: closing claim was an unsourced generalization ('Vendors use the word throttling for both behaviors'); replaced with the one vendor behavior I could verify, which is that API Gateway throttling rejects rather than queues
evidence: url: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-request-throttling.html - 'When request submissions exceed the steady-state request rate and burst limits, API Gateway begins to throttle requests. Clients may receive 429 Too Many Requests error responses at this point'
knowledge: a rejected request is not a queued one - a 429 returns immediately and leaves the retry decision with the client
notes: Rewritten stem is a genuine comparison and the price it names (latency, queue depth, timeouts on work still held) is specific rather than hedged.

fields.explanation: An origin shield is a shared cache layer between edge points of presence and the origin. Edge caching still runs in front of it: the shield sees only the misses, and it consolidates concurrent misses for the same object into as few as one origin fetch. The tier is not free - CloudFront charges separately for requests that pass through Origin Shield, and AWS itself calls it a poor fit for dynamic or rarely requested content, which would miss at both layers.

fields.explanation: The median describes the typical request while p99 exposes the slow tail. A p99 of 2 seconds bounds 99 requests in 100, not all of them, so it says nothing about how slow the worst ones get and does not mean every request lands between 50 ms and 2 seconds. At scale, even 1% can affect many requests and deserves investigation.
